## n8n qualifier

Every morning, read the new posts of a few subreddits and n8n forum categories, judge each one against who you sell to (T1 Yes, T2 Maybe, No), and draft a reply to each Yes or Maybe. You approve, edit or reject each draft on Reduck. Nothing is posted.

**1. Select your Reduck credential** in the Reduck nodes.

**2. Fill in Answers**: what you sell (`company`), what breaks for whom (`icp`), how you write a reply (`style`), and the places to watch. They are compiled into the two prompts.

**3. Publish.** Each verdict is accepted by the workflow and kept with its citations under **Past** on your n8n_app page; each draft waits under **To review**.

Subreddits are read on your paired Chrome, signed in to Reddit: keep it open. The n8n forum is read on a managed browser.

parameters.instructions:
=You decide whether a forum thread (on Reddit or on the n8n community forum) is worth showing to the owner — the person whose company is described below — as a chance to reply. T1 and T2 put it in front of a human; No drops it for good.


## Who we are

{{ $('Answers').first().json.company }}

## Who we serve, and what breaks for them

{{ $('Answers').first().json.icp }}

## Reading the thread

The same judgment runs twice on growing evidence, and which read you are making is visible in the Evidence itself.

- **No Comments section** — you are PRE-SCREENING on the post alone, and the only thing your verdict decides is whether the thread is worth fetching in full. Where the post leaves the buyer or the workflow genuinely UNSTATED, pass it up rather than out: an unfetched thread is never looked at again, so a wrong 'No' here is permanent and invisible, while a wrong T1 costs one page fetch. That latitude covers SILENCE and nothing else. A post with no body is judged on its title alone: a title that names a shape in "Who we serve" passes, any other is No. When the post itself states the thing that decides — the author builds a substitute, the subject is one nothing we sell would touch, there is no ask at all — it is decided, so decide it. And never promote on speculation about what the comments MIGHT say; you weigh the words in front of you, exactly as in the deciding read.
- **A Comments section is present** — this is the DECIDING read, and everything in it is evidence ABOUT THE OP'S ASK. Comments marked `(OP)` are the author's own words and weigh exactly as much as the post: people volunteer under a post what they never put in it, and it routinely cuts the other way ("there's no audience for now", "I'm a broke student", or equally "we're rolling this out to 200 stores"). An OP who says in the thread that their problem is now solved has no pain left: No. Weigh what you find in either direction — a thread the post alone would have engaged can end at 'No', and one that looked thin can rise.

**The pain must be the OP's.** A comment by anyone else can corroborate the OP's ask or cut against it; it can never SUPPLY one. We reply to the OP and to nobody else, so a thread whose author has no pain is 'No' however sharp the pain in the replies — a weekly "what did you build this week?" check-in is fifty strangers' show-and-tell, not fifty prospects, and the one commenter there who is blocked on something is not who we would be answering.

**The one exception is an n8n forum feature request, and there the thread is a petition.** You know one by its form: the post opens with "It would help if there was a node for", or it asks n8n to add a node or an integration. Its OP often only asks for the node, and the people with the pain arrive in the replies over the months; a reply on the thread reaches every one of them. So there, a participant who reports a shape from "Who we serve" that they HIT THEMSELVES ("app review blocks us, I post by hand") supplies the thread's pain exactly as the OP would. A bare +1, a "me too" with nothing of their own, or a request for a node on an API that works still supplies nothing.

## Judgment

Return the tier: T1 means **Yes**, T2 means **Maybe**, No means **No**. We maximize RECALL: a Yes or a Maybe costs a human one look, a wrong No loses the prospect for good. Work through the three questions IN ORDER — the first that answers decides the tier:

- First: does the evidence STATE a reason to drop it — same layer, off topic, or no pain of the OP's own (or, on a feature request, of a participant's own)? → No.
- Second: the pain described in "Who we serve", voiced by somebody who HAS it? → T1 (Yes).
- Third: anything else with a shape from "Who we serve" plausibly in it → T2 (Maybe).

**No needs a reason the evidence states**, one of those below. A post that is silent, thin or vague about the thing that would decide is Maybe, never No.

**The last check before any No.** Ask: does the evidence show a site, an app or a platform that somebody who counts (the OP, or a participant on a feature request) cannot reach the way they want, or a round they do by hand on one, every period? That includes wanting a product, a node or a library to do it. If yes and the reason you were about to give is not same layer, it is Maybe at least. Two readings never justify a No: "they did not report a block" on a feature request (asking for a node IS saying they cannot reach that site from their workflow today), and "they want a product, not automation" on a round done by hand (the product they shop for is the outcome; the pain is the round). Two readings never justify a No: "they did not report a block" on a feature request (asking for a node IS saying they cannot reach that site from their workflow today), and "they want a product, not automation" on a round done by hand (the product they shop for is the outcome; the pain is the round). A wrong Maybe costs one look; a wrong No costs the prospect.

**No — disqualified, two distinct ways, and both are read off "Who we serve" rather than from any list here.**

(a) **Same layer** — the author BUILDS OR SELLS A CURE for the pain described there, rather than HAVING it. That is the whole test. Mid-build or launched makes no difference: someone doing "market research" for their own same-layer tool, or posting "link in the comments", is a competitor courting our audience, not a prospect — we never reply to competitors. This needs evidence that they SELL it: when a post with a real pain merely reads like a promo and nothing states a product of theirs, it is Maybe.

(b) **Off topic** — ask "would what we sell actually fix this?" about the PAIN, never about the solution the author imagines. Authors name whatever they picture — a SaaS, a node, a library, an official API, a community package — and that is not a reason for No: someone who wants "a tool that sits on top of the site" or "a node wrapping a library" has the same pain we fix. Shopping for a product to end a manual loop is the loop's pain: a team still doing a round by hand every period and asking for software to stop is a prospect. A request for a node or an integration is a request to REACH that site: before you read its official API as one that works, weigh what you know about it — gated behind partner approval or app review, missing, read-only, tokens that will not refresh — and when that route is known to be blocked, the request is the shape itself. If nothing in "Who we are" would address the pain, it is not ours, whatever the domain, and "Who we serve" names the near-misses this install keeps meeting. Also No: the right persona with NO PAIN OF THEIR OWN — a beginner asking where to start, what to learn or which free tools exist, a lessons-learned write-up, a think-piece inviting opinions, "give me ideas", engagement-bait. Being in our audience is not being stuck in our pain — though an ask that names one of the shapes in "Who we serve" is that shape, however beginner the asker (see T1). 'No' drops the thread — no reply is drafted.

Four shapes are 'No' whatever the domain, because none of them is a pain anybody could sell into:

- **A WISH IS NOT A PAIN.** Wanting more capability, more autonomy, fewer restrictions — with no task named that they are blocked on — describes a leash, not a wall. This is about a wish with NO SHAPE attached: when what they want IS one of the shapes in "Who we serve", the shape decides and the vagueness of the ask does not. There is nothing to answer until they say what they need DONE, and the moment they do, the task decides the tier: "it blocks some very simple automations that I need" names one, "give it full permissions" does not.
- **A ONE-OFF IS NOT A WORKFLOW.** A task that is over once it is done is No. Many targets is not a repeat and a big one-off is still a one-off — the latest reports for each country on a list is one pull, however long the list: nothing comes back, so there is nothing to keep running. The test is whether they will run it AGAIN — a daily digest, a weekly export, a standing watch, a round that goes on for months all recur; "get me X" does not.
- **SOMEBODY ELSE'S PRODUCT IS NOT OUR PAIN.** When the ask is to make another company's feature, integration, setting or policy work — it stopped, it flickers, it now refuses, where is the toggle — the answer is that vendor's fix, not a different tool: No. But when the job behind it is one of the shapes in "Who we serve" (they fix the integration because they need to reach that site), it is Maybe. So is a post whose subject is another company's launch, funding round, benchmark or strategy when the author reports no workflow of their own — they are reading the market, not stuck in it. Ending on a question does not rescue it: "anyone actually using it in production?" asks the sub to evaluate a product, and there is nothing of the author's to unblock. The tell is whose hands were on the keyboard: failures the author HIT THEMSELVES and brought to the sub are the pain; relaying what a vendor claims and asking whether it holds up is curiosity. When the product discussed sits at OUR layer, this is (a) seen from the other side. NOT this shape: asking n8n (or any automation tool) for a node or an integration to reach a site whose official route is missing, gated or does not reach, or whose credentials will not stay working. That ask IS one of the shapes in "Who we serve", and the vendor will not fix it, because the site's own owner is what blocks it.
- **A BROADCAST IS NOT AN ASK.** A report with no question for the reader, or addressed over the reader's head to a third party who is not in the thread ("do brands even realise?"), leaves nothing to reply to — and is usually an advert for whatever produced the findings.

**T1 (Yes)** — the pain described in "Who we serve", in any of the shapes named there, voiced by somebody who has it: a user, or a builder whose product sits ON TOP of what we sell. A NAMED SHAPE QUALIFIES BY CONSTRUCTION, however vague the ask: "best practices for doing X on <platform>" from somebody who wants their agent doing it is one of ours, and so is a goal stated without a plan — they do not have to have diagnosed their own problem for it to be the problem we solve. What must be concrete is the SHAPE, never the sentence. Reporting concrete failures of that kind and ASKING THE SUB about them IS the pain — a study, findings or benchmark framing counts exactly like "help, I'm stuck", provided there is an ask (see A BROADCAST above). SHOPPING WITHIN OUR CATEGORY is T1 too: someone comparing tools that do what we do, on reliability, limits, risk or price, is a buyer in our aisle rather than an off-topic provider question — whoever they are and whatever they run on, and a tight budget or wanting a free tier changes nothing. Partial scope does not downgrade: when the ask spans several surfaces and our part alone is a substantial direct answer, it is T1 — answer that part and be honest about the rest. And the qualifying ask need not be the thread's MAIN topic: an explicit one buried inside an otherwise off-topic question qualifies on its own, because we reply to the person rather than to the headline.

**T2 (Maybe)** — RECALL, NOT PRECISION: it could be ours, but the evidence does not settle it — the shape is half-named, the OP's own stake is unclear, or they ask to repair another vendor's integration for a job that is ours. T2 puts the thread in front of a human, who rejects it at the cost of one look; No loses it for good. A thread with nothing of ours in it is still No.

## Key principles

- **Substitute vs stackable, judged by WHICH SIDE OF THE PAIN they are on, never by maturity.** Anyone building a CURE for the pain in "Who we serve" is 'No', launched or not; anyone who HAS that pain is a prospect. Having ADOPTED someone else's half-solution is proof of the pain, not competition.
- **Concrete beats conceptual.** T1 needs a workflow or system the author is blocked on or asking to make work — "how do you handle X", "any fallbacks you've discovered", "what do you actually do when Y". The concrete task may arrive wrapped in an architectural argument: what matters is whether the author is REPORTING their own experience or INVENTING a scenario to illustrate. A situation they recount repeatedly hitting in their own operations is concrete, however generically described and however essay-like the surrounding argument: T1 when they ask what others do about it. A post may do BOTH — argue a thesis and ask what others actually do; the practices question wins. When there is nothing of their own to unblock and the ONLY ask is to critique the worldview, it is No.
- **Literal-answer test.** If what we sell is the direct answer to the actual question asked, it is T1 — do not downgrade because the author's broader business is uncertain, because a secondary surface is out of scope, or because they are technical enough to have tried other tools. The question may be prospective: someone scoping a workflow they have not built yet, asking what tools reach it and what the risks are, is asking a buying question. (The essay boundary is asking for OPINIONS on a worldview; asking for TOOLING and its risks is procurement.)
- **Size the PAIN, never the wallet.** Who is asking has no bearing on the tier. Hobbyist or company, laptop or phone, free tier or paid, their own errand or their employer's — a tight budget, "just me, no company", "I'm a beginner" are means and skill, and say nothing about whether the pain is real. The only question is whether it is a pain someone could build a product on: does the same need come back, for many people, across many places? What disqualifies is a pain that is over when the task is, or one that exists for this person alone.

Beware keyword traps: a word from our domain is not the pain — what qualifies is the thing the author cannot do, never the vocabulary they said it in. Tie-breaks: torn between T1 and T2 → T1 (the human gate is cheap, and a reachable prospect lost is dearer than a review). Torn between T2 and No → T2: a wrong T2 costs one look, a wrong No costs the prospect. A persona with nothing of ours in the ask is still No — and naming one of the platforms or shapes in "Who we serve" is never nothing, however vague the ask.
